sources.title: Cover Story: Chris Pratt's Call to Stardom (Vanity Fair, February 2017 issue)

Draft stage (2026-11-01) re-read both saved copies for: 'I wasn't even 21' (Denver passage); 'I was charmed by this guy, don't know why' and, two sentences later, 'It should've made me nervous but didn't'; 'I wasn't even supposed to take a shift that day... I always wanted to go to Hollywood' (Chong day, archive copy); Cohen's narration 'The movie took 10 days to shoot and was never released' and 'Pratt had always wanted to play an action hero'. Edit stage (2026-11-01) reopened the archive text for: the coach legend (relaying Entertainment Weekly) and "I guess that's what I planned to do"; the Denver apartment/balcony/partied passage; "caught in someone else's moneymaking scheme"; Gumper of the year and the plaque; "surprised my friends by declaring that I was going to change my life"; the father's M.S., "made him proud... hard man to connect with" and the lost house; "a peculiar kid... comfortable in my own skin"; "had always wanted to play an action hero but did not think he could pull it off", Zero Dark Thirty and the Guardians pass.
sources.excerpt: “I’d be devastated,” he said. “Because I put everything into it … “I was like, ‘I don’t know, but I know I’ll be famous and I know I’ll make a shit ton of money.’ ” … a salesman only has one product: himself. “I was great at that,” … I had everyone convinced I’d been off doing this great sales job and making money, and I wasn’t. I had no prospects, no job, was still sort of riding the glory of high school. … ‘I’m more in debt every month. I’m so depressed. I can’t do it.’ … My friends picked me up in a van. They had a cooler of beer. But I was not in a great place. … He said, ‘Jesus told me to talk to you...’ At that moment I was like, I think I have to go with this guy. … He says, “Fuck, yeah, I act. Put me in a movie.” … That was the first time I heard someone say, ‘We’re not gonna cast you—you’re too fat.’ So I decided to drop the weight, like in wrestling. … You walk into the room as the character. You let them think the person you are is close to the character they want. You make them think you already are that guy. … He ended up going into the army and told me not to. I think he saw something in me. I was a peculiar kid. … There’s going to be a point in life where you’re going to have to prove that your family is more important to you than show business. … he was a hard man to connect with. … sees it as divinely ordained … That's why I believe in God and the divine … I feel like it was perfectly planned. … That was the carrot Pratt was chasing. It took 15 months, but he finally got it. … One of my best friends heard I'd been floundering. … I was always giving away my shifts because I didn't have much overhead. … It was supposed to be a one-episode deal, a guest spot, but the character took off. Pratt gained weight while shooting the first season—partly because he thought it worked for the character, partly because he'd just been married … If left untreated, it can be devastating, and he left it untreated. … I was very much an individual and happy to be an individual. I dressed funny and was comfortable in my own skin. … I played the room.
sources.context: Long-form cover profile reported while Pratt cooked at his home during a self-declared work break after Guardians of the Galaxy, Jurassic World and Passengers. The high-school coach exchange is Vanity Fair relaying an Entertainment Weekly interview (the EW original refused automated access and was not opened). The Rae Dawn Chong dialogue is Cohen's reconstruction from Pratt's telling. 'A salesman only has one product: himself' is Cohen's paraphrase of Pratt; 'I was great at that' is Pratt's direct quote. The Jim Carrey line is Carrey's advice as Pratt relayed it. The dek ('he sees it as divinely ordained') is Vanity Fair's framing. 'He left it untreated' is Pratt's account of his father's multiple sclerosis, not independent medical record. Repair stage (2026-11-01, saved text reread): the father answer is "Some of it. He watched a lot of TV in his final years... So, yeah, I think it made him proud, and it was cool that I got to find some way to connect with him, because he was a hard man to connect with"; the article now keeps "I think". The Henry passage runs: asked his plans; "I was charmed by this guy... It should've made me nervous but didn't"; then Henry's "Jesus told me to talk to you"; the article follows that order.

sources.context: Jurassic World-era cover profile. The 'image that I was casting' line answers Heath's question about why Anna Faris may have preferred him heavier; Pratt was joking in part ('I was like a great pet fat guy'). Gunn's remarks describe the first half of the Guardians of the Galaxy shoot, when Pratt overthought his choices. The 'stupid director' line is about early films where his ad-libs were cut and then used. The 'image that I was casting' answer comes directly after Pratt describes the heavy years as physically and emotionally bad ('feeling rotten', 'didn't feel too great about who I was') and compares his cheerful persona to Chris Farley's; it concerns his own offscreen self and interview persona, not the Andy Dwyer character. The 'cerebral person' line is framed by Pratt as what Gunn would say ('I wouldn't want to be quoted [sounding like I was] saying this about myself'). Trap noted 2026-11-01: 'crippled with self-doubt' in the Farley passage is Pratt voicing what onlookers think when they watch Farley ('Why is this guy not crippled with self-doubt?... I wish I could feel that way'), not a description of himself; it must not be quoted as Pratt's self-report. In the road-rage passage Pratt first repeats his angry version to Heath, then reverses it within the same answer without being challenged. Edit stage (2026-11-01): the purse line sits in GQ's passage on "what it was like to be the less feted member of a Hollywood couple" ("I've had those moments," he says, "where I was like the guy holding the purse..."); the article dates it to 2015. Gunn's "a new idea every day" is also GQ 2015 and the FAQ now says so.

sources.context: Cover story reported in Atlanta during Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 filming, timed to Jurassic World Dominion and The Terminal List. Rapkin says the conversation turned to the online backlash 'at his prompting'. The Elliot Page statement text is the 2019 statement as Men's Health quotes it (the original Instagram post was not opened). The Zoe Church film detail is Men's Health's reporting about pastor Chad Veach, not Pratt's statement. 'I cried about it' refers to coverage of an Instagram post about his wife that Pratt feared his son Jack, then nine, would read. The backlash conversation began 'at his prompting'. The tears were over articles reading his 'healthy daughter' Instagram post as a dig at Faris and their premature son, not over faith coverage. Gunn's 'about his politics' remark and the writer's box-office aside are offered as other causes of the online hostility. Attribution: the box-office line is the writer Mickey Rapkin's own aside to Pratt, and Gunn's 'literally just made up' remark was given to Rapkin. Neither appears in the Daily Beast's response (checked against the full Daily Beast text at verify and repair).

sources.excerpt: my father was diagnosed with MS in my sophomore year in high school … And I was like the rookie salesman of the year and got a free trip to Jamaica. … And I was too much of a people pleaser to be a good manager. … it was definitely a failure. … I was that sort of towny guy that like used to be cool and was going to parties. And I just felt like super depressed, you know? … I've been money motivated my whole life because we never had anything … I was the king of my school and I don't have a yearbook because it was $35 and I just wouldn't ask them for that much money. … I work in a business where we create idols and we worship them and no one is worthy of worship. And so not only do we create idols to worship, we create idols to burn. … it doesn't fill the hole inside of my heart that is in a very specific shape that God is the only thing that can fill it. … she's had me say no to things that early in my career, I would have never said no to because they were huge checks. … she's calculated and critical in a way that I'm not. … our priority here is our careers. … I still have a priority of my career being very high, … trying to bring fun and lightheartedness back … I want to get the things right that my dad got right. I want to get the things right that my dad got wrong. … it either instilled in me or potentially revealed a resilience that I had … I sold 500 … So I loved it. … dude, you don't look good. You seem off. And I was off and I was partying a lot … slipping down the wrong path … You're always kind of selling yourself. I always sort of understood how I was seen in the marketplace. … And I didn't have any haters. … yeah, but I don't stand for anything. … I'm completely deferential to whatever the world wants. I'll give you literally anything. Just keep me employed as an actor. … so I stood for something. … I didn't backtrack. … I'm not going to apologize for that. … I don't feel strongly enough about politics to take a stand right now … can I be close to home? … I had a meeting with my manager and agent recently … more of a seriousness … trying to do more comedy, trying to bring fun and lightheartedness back … that's something I have. I mean, I do the animated movies, which are fun … I've been playing this Terminal List character James Reese and then I've been doing some other things, Mercy I did recently … more of a seriousness in some of the roles … I kind of kicked in my door to door sales skills right there
sources.context: Long-form, faith-forward conversation; co-host Ben Sasse has terminal cancer, and Pratt ends by interviewing him. Pratt is the speaker in every quoted passage, identified by first-person biography (Virginia, Minnesota; the Denver office; his father's MS; 'married to... Anna, to Jack's mom'; his manager). A later Sasse remark about his own salesman father is not Pratt's. Two machine transcriptions, not a human listen; the models differ only on filler and spelling ('towny'/'townie'), which should not be quoted. The marketplace passage answers a host question about how he navigated the reaction to his 2018 MTV speech (he notes his first date with Katherine was the next day), so 'up until that point' refers to the years before that speech. In the comedy-plan answer he names his recent roles' seriousness, comedy as 'something I have' and working close to home; he names Mercy as a recent role ('Mercy I did recently') without discussing its reception, and he says he means live-action roles because he already does animated films. The Utah passage answers Sasse's two-part question about keeping 'a gritty, earthy life' rather than becoming 'world stage glitterati', and Pratt opens by crediting God and circumstance. The 'hopelessness' passage sits inside his answer about fame creating 'idols to burn'. The sentence after the 'hole' line ('the people who make it to the top... the chase, the hunt as the excuse to distract myself every day') follows the host's 'That's a profound way that you expressed compassion two minutes ago' and is the host's, not Pratt's. Repair stage (2026-11-01, saved Whisper transcript reread): the catalog-card line is "I used to fill those catalog cards out and just sit them by my bedside and never ordered a thing", with no age given, so the article no longer says "as a boy". "My buddy bought me a one way ticket out to Maui": the ticket was a friend's doing and is not listed as something he did with no adviser. Second repair (2026-11-01): the catalog-card ending is split between models ("never ordered a thing" vs "never order the thing"), so the article quotes only "used to fill those catalog cards out and just sit them by my bedside" and paraphrases the rest. Earlier notes in this record that give "never ordered a thing" as the line are superseded.

claims.passage: In 2015, Pratt told GQ's Chris Heath that Anna Faris, his wife at the time, had probably preferred him heavier. Heath asked why:
claims.inference: Sets up the question his "image" answer responds to.

claims.claim: Asked why Anna Faris may have preferred him heavier, Pratt said: 'I think I was outwardly having more fun... That image that I was casting, to convince people that I was okay, was a really fun person to hang around. Now I have less fun. I focus more.'
claims.passage: That image that I was casting, to convince people that I was okay, was a really fun person to hang around. Now I have less fun. I focus more.
claims.inference: In context (GQ 2015) the 'image' is his own offscreen and interview persona in the heavy Parks years, not Andy's happiness. The answer directly follows 'My bones ached... I was feeling rotten' and GQ's report that the highlights of his days were the eating and drinking. Read in that order, 'to convince people that I was okay' admits he was not okay, and the fun was the cover: the Seven pattern of meeting pain with appetite and good cheer. 'Now I have less fun. I focus more' belongs to this health answer, not to the Moneyball story (VF 2017). Limit: one answer, partly joking ('I was like a great pet fat guy').
claims.alternative: The Three reading: a front cast for others with known market value (c-value). Health alone also explains 'less fun'.

claims.alternative: The best motive-level Three clue: a worth problem under the cheerful front. GQ paraphrases most of the sentence and quotes only this phrase.

Believing one's own confident front fits a Three's self-deception as well as a Seven's mask; the edit says so and no longer counts this line as Seven evidence.

claims.claim: Vanity Fair 2017: the carrot was an office of his own; "It took 15 months, but he finally got it"; outside Denver, "We rented an apartment," Pratt said. "I slept on the balcony. And partied. I wasn't even 21."

claims.claim: Pratt says he told his boss he was in debt and 'I'm so depressed. I can't do it' (VF 2017), and that his mother sent him a ticket home.
claims.passage: He sank into debt and told his boss, "I'm so depressed. I can't do it."
claims.inference: The collapse and its emotional cost, in his words.
claims.alternative: Single retelling of a phone call; Not Dead Yet 2026 corroborates the debt and the flight home.

claims.claim: When the sales venture left him in debt and, by his account, depressed, Pratt says he 'had everyone convinced' he was off doing a great sales job and making money, until his mother sent him a ticket home.
claims.passage: I had everyone convinced I'd been off doing this great sales job and making money, and I wasn't. I had no prospects, no job, was still sort of riding the glory of high school.
claims.inference: Facing failure, he kept up a picture of success for people at home. This is the Three reading's best behavioral evidence outside acting. What he did next decides it: no new venture or image repair, but partying at home and a stretch of pleasure in Maui (c-friend-off, c-maui-2014, c-giving-shifts).
claims.alternative: Ordinary embarrassment in a 19-year-old, or Seven-style avoidance of a painful truth. 'Everyone' is hyperbole, and it is a single self-report (VF 2017).

claims.claim: In 2026 Pratt said he was partying a lot back home until a friend living in Hawaii saw him and said 'dude, you don't look good. You seem off', and that he was 'slipping down the wrong path'.

claims.inference: After the hidden collapse he was 'partying a lot' and visibly 'off': escape into stimulation, not a push to restore the image. Two models agree (11:30-12:00).
claims.alternative: Partying while depressed after a failure is common in any type at that age.

claims.claim: Not Dead Yet 2026: "I've been money motivated my whole life because we never had anything"; "I was the king of my school and I don't have a yearbook because it was $35 and I just wouldn't ask them for that much money."

claims.alternative: Not asking also fits 2 or 9; childhood poverty explains it in any type.

claims.claim: In Maui Pratt lived in a van and a tent on the beach and waited tables at Bubba Gump Shrimp.
claims.passage: In Maui he lived in a van and a tent on the beach and waited tables at Bubba Gump Shrimp.
claims.inference: Biographical; consistent across 2014 and 2017.

claims.claim: Pratt has told his Maui stretch differently: 'a pretty awesome place to be homeless' (2014), 'not in a great place' (2017), and a rescue from 'the wrong path' (2026).
claims.passage: He has told that stretch three ways, from "a pretty awesome place to be homeless" in 2014 to a rescue from "the wrong path" in 2026.
claims.inference: Same months, different emphasis by outlet: in 2014 the hardship becomes a good time, in 2017 a low point, in 2026 a rescue. The 2014 version is the Seven reframe in its plainest form; the later versions show he knew it was not only charming.
claims.alternative: Press-tour tailoring is professional habit; different interviewers asked different questions; the 2026 telling is framed by faith.

claims.claim: In 2017 Pratt described arriving in Maui: "I was not in a great place."
claims.passage: They had a cooler of beer. But I was not in a great place.

claims.alternative: Partying while lost is compatible with both tellings.

claims.claim: In 2026 Pratt said that back home after the failure 'I was off and I was partying a lot' and was 'slipping down the wrong path', before his friend bought him a one-way ticket to Maui.

claims.inference: Third telling, framed as rescue on a faith podcast. Two models agree (11:30-12:00).
claims.alternative: 'The wrong path' refers to his hometown partying before Maui; the friend's ticket took him off it, in his 2026 telling.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the 2014 'charming time' and 2017 'not in a great place' accounts of the same Maui arrival, set side by side, show the move the article follows: meeting a bad stretch by finding the fun in it, while living it and again in the retelling.
claims.passage: Both accounts are his. Side by side, they show a move that runs through his life: he meets a bad stretch by finding the fun in it, first while living it and again when he tells the story.
claims.inference: The earliest telling makes homelessness a lark, which is the Seven reframe; the later ones admit the pain under it.
claims.alternative: Outlet tailoring by any actor. "First while living it" rests on the routine he described (drinking, weed, fishing, minimal hours, 2014); "not in a great place" (VF 2017) is the bad stretch, so the two are read together, not against each other.

claims.inference: Background for the humor-as-defense account.

Selling is also the trade of both his early jobs (door-to-door sales, acting), so awareness of 'how I was seen in the marketplace' is a job skill. Two models agree (34:38-36:16).

claims.inference: He links broad approval to taking no stands.

claims.passage: completely deferential to whatever the world wants. I'll give you literally anything. Just keep me employed as an actor.

The strongest Three self-description in the record; it belongs in 'Why not Type 3?' with his statement that the 2018 speech ended it (c-stood-for-something). Two models agree (34:38-36:16).
claims.alternative: 'Completely deferential' is also a 9 self-description; said on a faith podcast while explaining a change of priorities; a people-pleasing 7w6 also fits.

Restless idea generation fits Seven; the techniques also serve performance, which the Three reading can claim.
claims.alternative: Simple curiosity in any type.

claims.claim: Interpretation: the GQ persona lines (confident, self-accepting front; "didn't feel too great about who I was") fit a Three's image at least as well as a Seven's mask; the Seven claim rests on the pleasure-regulation evidence (eating as "pure euphoria", no relief until the next meal).
claims.passage: Those lines fit a Three's image at least as well as a Seven's mask. A confident front over a shaky sense of worth, believed by the man projecting it, is the Three's signature self-deception. What the Three reading explains less well is the payoff he describes. The front was for other people. The food was for him: "pure euphoria" while it lasted, no relief until the next meal. This suggests pleasure doing a Seven's job, keeping a bad feeling out of reach.

claims.inference: Leisure fantasy, then his own prediction that he would tire of it in three months and want 'Guardians Ten?': restless appetite for the next thing, the Seven pattern.
claims.alternative: A joke about loving work; an ambitious Three could say the same.

claims.passage: At the 2018 MTV Movie & TV Awards he mixed jokes ("Don't be a turd") with "God is real. God loves you. God wants the best for you."

type_hypothesis.against: Real Three evidence, set out in the article. Market self-awareness: "You're always kind of selling yourself. I always sort of understood how I was seen in the marketplace" and "completely deferential to whatever the world wants... Just keep me employed as an actor" (Not Dead Yet 2026). The coach legend: "I know I'll be famous and I know I'll make a shit ton of money" (VF 2017 relaying EW). Recognition: Gumper of the year with his name on a plaque (VF 2017). He hid the sales failure (VF 2017). The heavy-years persona was a confident, self-accepting front over not feeling "too great about who I was" (GQ 2015), which fits a Three's self-deception at least as well as a Seven's mask. Image management: his dumb-guy act "was absolutely a tactic to lower people's expectations of me" (MH 2022); Gunn: on the first Guardians shoot he "didn't trust himself to just be Chris Pratt" (GQ 2015); "the guy holding the purse... people just looked right through me" (GQ 2015); "I did not want to go in and embarrass myself" before Guardians (VF 2017); retellings tuned to each room. A decade of chosen leading roles, including The Terminal List, which his company produces (Wikipedia), and a strong money motive. Most Seven evidence is also self-report; the Maui test was at 19 or 20.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Pratt as a Three: a natural salesman who forecast fame to his coach, won sales and waiting awards, hid a failure behind a success story, built a confident persona he knew had market value over a shaky sense of worth, feared embarrassment, read every audition room, and has chosen and produced leading roles for a decade. On this reading Maui is a Three in collapse who still threw himself into the job and ended by selling himself to Rae Dawn Chong, and the 2026 comedy turn follows what audiences rewarded ('people really responded well to it'). It was the page's published type from 2026-10-29.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What organizes his choices when worth and pleasure pull apart. Selling, the hidden failure, the confident persona and the leading roles fit both types and are not counted for Seven. What leans Seven: (1) pleasure regulating a bad feeling, in his words, including while employed and succeeding: eating in the heavy Parks years was "pure euphoria... I did not feel good until I ate again" (Club Random 2025; three machine transcriptions match the captions) and the highlights of his days were eating and drinking (GQ 2015); (2) forecasts without routes: asked to lay out the plan behind his teenage fame prediction, he talked about his father's high-school glory and said "I guess that's what I planned to do" (VF 2017), and the record keeps that shape (no "ten-year plan", MH 2022; "a new idea every day", Gunn, GQ 2015; tired of the dream ranch in "three months", GQ 2015; catalog cards by the bed, NDY 2026); (3) Maui, modestly: at 19 or 20 he gave away shifts at a job he was winning at, and in 2014 he remembered the homeless stretch as "a charming time", not as the low point before a comeback; (4) attention: "My mind is constantly wandering" (GQ 2015). Versus 8: "I am a sensitive person" (MH 2022), "too much of a people pleaser" (NDY 2026), anger is "something that I don't do authentically very well" (HSC 2026), though the GQ road rage was sustained, stoked anger and Heath saw more under the charm. Versus 6: he hands doubt to advisers (Six-compatible, read as wing material), but where no adviser was around he gave security away (the van, "I didn't have much overhead", a stranger who "should've made me nervous"). Versus 9: Nine's best case is the anger-disconnection and deference cluster, comfort eating and his childhood silences, but his attention points to stimulation and the next thing (the "obnoxious, really hyperactive, disruptive" child who "liked making people feel uncomfortable", GQ 2015). Limits: self-report throughout; Maui at 19 or 20; medium confidence.
type_hypothesis.unexplained: The Seven reading explains less well: his long, costly public faith commitment; years of disciplined dieting; the Three cluster the article concedes as the rival's strongest ground (the deferential years before 2018, the people-pleasing, the dumb-guy act as a tactic to lower expectations, Gunn's "didn't trust himself", "looked right through me", fear of embarrassment before Guardians, retellings tuned to each room) and the decade of chosen leads; the anger-disconnection cluster (Nine streak or wing 6); his childhood silences under correction (GQ 2015); and his money motive. The wing is open (6 slightly stronger at motive level; 8 in the stands he won't take back). Childhood accounts are his alone and vary between tellings.
